about: Parts of NASA's Mars rovers for Seebra's example 'Mars rovers up close'. Positions x, y, z: metres on a simplified model of each rover (x forward, y up, z left), not exact. Masses and power only where a source states them.

rovers.name: Sojourner
rovers.note: Planned for 7 sols, worked 83. Talked to Mars only through the Pathfinder lander's radio.

rovers.name: Spirit & Opportunity
rovers.power_source: Solar arrays, 1.3 m² of triple-junction cells
rovers.computer: RAD6000, 20 MHz; 128 MB RAM, 256 MB flash
rovers.note: Twins planned for 90 sols. Dust on the arrays cut the energy per sol; wind 'cleaning events' restored it. Opportunity ran 14 years and drove a marathon.

rovers.name: Curiosity
rovers.power_source: MMRTG: plutonium-238 decay heat to electricity
rovers.battery: Two lithium-ion, 42 Ah each (for peaks above the RTG's output)
rovers.computer: RAD750, 200 MHz; 256 MB RAM, 2 GB flash (two, one spare)
rovers.note: Too heavy for airbags: lowered by the sky crane. The RTG's output falls slowly as the plutonium decays (half-life 88 years) and the thermocouples age.

rovers.name: Perseverance
rovers.power_source: MMRTG: plutonium-238 decay heat to electricity
rovers.computer: RAD750, 200 MHz (plus a vision computer for driving)
rovers.note: Built on Curiosity's design. Collects rock cores in sealed tubes for a future sample return, and carried the Ingenuity helicopter.

parts.detail: 0.22 m² of gallium arsenide cells on the roof: about 16 W at Martian noon, enough to drive or run the spectrometer, not both at once.
Lithium–thionyl chloride D cells, 150 Wh, not rechargeable: kept in reserve for when the sun was low.
Two black-and-white cameras, 768 × 484 pixels, with laser stripe projectors to see rocks in front of the wheels.
One colour camera at the back, to see where the spectrometer was placed.
Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer: curium-244 sources bombard a rock; the returned particles and X-rays give its elements. Placed against rocks like Barnacle Bill and Yogi.
UHF modem and whip antenna: everything went through the Pathfinder lander, never straight to Earth.
Insulated box with three radioisotope heater units (about 1 W of heat each) around the electronics.
Six 13 cm wheels on a rocker-bogie suspension, first flown here and used by every NASA rover since. Top speed 1 cm/s.
Intel 80C85: semi-autonomous hazard avoidance between commands from Earth.
1.3 m² of triple-junction cells on the deck and its wings: about 140 W at noon and 900 Wh per sol at landing; dust brought that down until wind cleaned them.
Two lithium-ion batteries, 8 Ah each, inside the warm electronics box.
Two cameras on the mast, 1024 × 1024 pixels with 8 filters each, at eye height (1.5 m): the rovers' famous panoramas and sundials.
Black-and-white stereo cameras beside Pancam with a wider view, for planning where to drive.
Fisheye stereo pairs low at the front and back, for autonomous hazard avoidance.
Miniature Thermal Emission Spectrometer in the mast's base, looking out through a periscope: minerals from their infrared spectra at a distance.
On the arm's turret: 30 µm per pixel close-ups of rock and soil grains.
On the turret: curium-244 sources and an X-ray detector, like Sojourner's but improved.
On the turret: a cobalt-57 source reveals which iron minerals are present. It found jarosite at Meridiani, a mineral that forms in water.
On the turret: grinds a 45 mm wide, up to 5 mm deep hole so the instruments see fresh rock.
A steerable X-band dish for direct links to the Deep Space Network; most data went through orbiters by UHF.
Eight radioisotope heater units in the warm electronics box.
RAD6000 at 20 MHz with 128 MB RAM and 256 MB flash. Spirit's flash filled up 18 sols in, and a remote fix revived it.
Each wheel has its own motor; top speed 5 cm/s. Spirit dragged a stuck front wheel backwards for years.

Multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator: about 2,000 W of heat from 4.8 kg of plutonium dioxide becomes about 110 W of electricity, around 2.5 kWh per sol, with no dependence on sun or dust. Its waste heat warms the rover.
Two lithium-ion batteries, 42 Ah each, charged by the MMRTG: driving and instruments draw more than it makes, for a while.
Two cameras on the mast, 34 mm and 100 mm focal length, 1600 × 1200 pixels, colour and HD video.
Fires a 1067 nm laser at rocks up to 7 m away and reads the spark's light (laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy); a telescope camera (RMI) images the spot.
Two stereo pairs (one spare) on the mast head, black and white.
Rover Environmental Monitoring Station (Spain): two booms on the mast measure wind, air and ground temperature, pressure, humidity and UV.
Four pairs, front and back, low on the body.
Mars Hand Lens Imager on the arm: colour close-ups down to 14 µm per pixel, and the rover's selfies.
On the turret, a successor of Sojourner's and the MER's spectrometers (Canada).
A percussive drill makes rock powder that CHIMRA sieves and portions into the instruments on the deck.
Sample Analysis at Mars: a mass spectrometer, gas chromatograph and laser spectrometer in about 40 kg, the largest instrument. Found organic molecules and seasonal methane.
Chemistry and Mineralogy: X-ray diffraction of drilled powder, the first on another planet; it showed Gale crater's lake mudstones.
Dynamic Albedo of Neutrons (Russia): pulses neutrons into the ground and counts what comes back, sensing hydrogen down to about 1 m.
Radiation Assessment Detector: the surface dose a human would get, measured since the cruise to Mars.
Mars Descent Imager under the body: colour video of the descent.
X-band, steerable; most data relays through orbiters by UHF.
Two RAD750s at 200 MHz (one spare), 256 MB RAM and 2 GB flash each.
Rocker-bogie again. Sharp rocks punctured the thin skins, so drives were replanned around them.
The same kind as Curiosity's: about 110 W of electricity from plutonium-238, around 2.5 kWh per sol.
Two lithium-ion batteries, 43 Ah each.
Two zoom cameras (26–110 mm), 1600 × 1200 pixels, on the mast: the rover's eyes for science and panoramas.
LIBS and Raman spectroscopy with lasers up to 7 m away, infrared spectra, a colour camera, and a microphone that records the laser's snaps (and Mars' wind).
20-megapixel colour navigation cameras on the mast head.
Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer (Spain): wind, temperature, pressure, humidity, radiation and dust, on the mast and deck.
Colour, higher resolution than Curiosity's, front and back.
Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry on the turret: X-ray fluorescence maps of elements at sub-millimetre spots.
A deep-UV Raman and fluorescence spectrometer for organics and minerals, with the WATSON close-up camera, on the turret.
Cuts finger-sized rock cores into sample tubes, instead of making powder as Curiosity's drill does.
In the belly: a small internal robot arm moves, images, seals and stores the cores. Some tubes were left on the ground as a depot for a future sample return.
Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment: split CO₂ into oxygen by solid-oxide electrolysis, 122 g in 16 runs, about as much as a small dog breathes in 10 hours.
Ground-penetrating radar (Norway) at the rear: layers down to about 10 m as the rover drives.

parts.role: The first powered flight on another planet
parts.detail: 1.8 kg helicopter with 1.2 m rotors, carried under the belly and dropped off in April 2021. It flew 72 times until a rotor broke in January 2024; its solar panel charged batteries that gave about 350 W in flight.
X-band, steerable, like Curiosity's; most data relays through orbiters by UHF.
The RAD750 runs the rover; a separate computer processes images while driving, so it drives while it thinks.
Narrower, thicker-skinned aluminium wheels with curved treads, after Curiosity's punctures.
